sentences.text: You are walking down a busy street.
Hundreds of faces pass you by.
And then, for no reason you can explain, one of them stops you.
Your heart speeds up.
Your pupils widen.
Your palms get a little warm.
Something inside you whispers: look again.
You did not decide this.
Your brain decided it for you, in less than a second, long before you had a single conscious thought.
So what just happened?
Why is a man drawn to a woman at all?
Why her, and not someone else?
The answer is a strange mix of ancient evolution, invisible chemistry, a brain on fire, and the culture you grew up in.
Let us take attraction apart, piece by piece, and see what is really going on inside you.
Part One.
The Oldest Story on Earth.
To understand attraction, we have to go back.
Way back.
About one billion years.
For most of the history of life, living things simply copied themselves.
A cell split in two.
Then those two split again.
Simple.
Efficient.
But there was a problem.
A copy is only ever as good as the original.
And the world is full of enemies.
Viruses.
Parasites.
Bacteria.
They evolve fast, and they are constantly searching for weaknesses.
A population of identical copies is a buffet.
Once a parasite cracks the code of one, it can crack all of them.
So life invented something radical.
Mixing.
Instead of copying itself, an organism could combine its genes with someone else's genes.
Every child would be a brand new combination.
A new lock that the parasites had never seen before.
This was the birth of sex.
And with it came two different strategies.
One partner made tiny cells that were cheap and plentiful.
We call them sperm.
The other made large cells that were rare and full of resources.
We call them eggs.
In humans, the difference is enormous.
A man produces millions of sperm every single day.
A woman is born with all the eggs she will ever have, and only around four hundred of them will mature in her lifetime.
And then comes pregnancy.
Nine months of carrying a child, followed by years of feeding and care.
For most of human history, that was a huge investment of energy, time, and risk.
This imbalance shaped everything.
Evolution built men and women with slightly different instincts, because their bodies faced different challenges.
Attraction is the engine that drives the oldest story on Earth: the story of genes trying to survive into the future.
But here is the important part.
Your genes do not care about your feelings.
They do not give you a plan.
They give you a feeling.
A pull.
A spark.
And you experience that spark as attraction.
Part Two.
What the Eyes Are Looking For.
So what exactly is a man's brain scanning for when he looks at a woman?
Scientists have studied this across dozens of cultures, and some patterns appear again and again.
The first is health.
For our ancestors, a healthy partner meant healthy children.
But nobody could run a blood test.
So the brain learned to read signals of health directly from the body.
Clear skin.
Bright eyes.
Shiny hair.
Full lips.
These are not random preferences.
Many of them are signs of youth, good nutrition, and a strong immune system.
Then there is symmetry.
As you grew in your mother's womb, your body was built from a genetic blueprint.
But stress, illness, and parasites can push that building process slightly off course.
A face that grew up perfectly balanced can be a sign that the body handled those challenges well.
In experiments, when people are shown faces that have been made more symmetrical by a computer, they usually rate them as more attractive.
Most of the time, people have no idea why.
Next comes something surprising.
Average.
When researchers blend dozens of faces together into one composite face, the result is almost always rated as more attractive than the individual faces.
Not boring.
Attractive.
An average face may signal a mix of many genes, and a smaller chance of rare genetic problems.
And then there are hormones written on the body.
As a girl becomes a woman, the hormone estrogen reshapes her body.
It softens the face, makes the lips fuller, and changes how fat is stored, giving many women a waist that is narrower than their hips.
Across many cultures, men are drawn to this waist to hip ratio.
Not one exact body type, but a shape that signals that the hormones of adulthood are working.
All of these signals are processed in a fraction of a second, deep in the brain, without permission.
You do not think: this face is symmetrical.
You just think: wow.
Part Three.
The Invisible Signals.
But attraction is not only about what you see.
Some of the most powerful signals are things you cannot see at all.
Let us start with the voice.
When men listen to recordings of women's voices, they often rate higher, softer voices as more attractive.
A higher voice can be linked to higher levels of estrogen.
Some studies even suggest that a woman's voice can become slightly higher and more attractive around the most fertile days of her cycle.
The effect is small, and scientists still debate it.
But the ear may be quietly listening for information the eyes cannot see.
Then there is smell.
You might think humans have a weak sense of smell compared to dogs.
And you would be right.
But our noses are still collecting information all the time.
In a famous experiment, women were asked to smell T-shirts that men had worn for two nights.
On average, they preferred the smell of men whose immune system genes were different from their own.
Why would that matter?
Because a child who inherits two different sets of immune genes may be able to recognize a wider range of diseases.
Your nose might be helping you choose a partner who completes your defenses.
There are also claims about human pheromones, invisible chemical messages that make people instantly attracted.
Many perfume companies love this idea.
But the truth is that scientists have not found a clear, proven human sex pheromone yet.
Smell matters.
Magic perfumes, probably not.
So attraction is a whole body experience.
Your eyes, your ears, and your nose are all sending reports to one place.
Your brain.
Part Four.
Your Brain on Fire.
The moment you see someone attractive, your brain lights up like a city at night.
Deep inside, a small region called the hypothalamus sends a signal to your body.
Your heart beats faster.
Your blood pressure rises.
Your pupils widen to let in more light, so you can see the person better.
At the same time, your brain releases a chemical called dopamine.
Dopamine is the molecule of wanting.
It is the same chemical that is released when you eat something delicious, win a game, or get a notification on your phone.
It does not make you happy, exactly.
It makes you want more.
This is why attraction feels like a pull.
Your brain has flagged this person as a reward, and it wants you to go after that reward.
If the attraction grows into something stronger, the brain chemistry becomes even more intense.
Brain scans of people who are newly in love show something remarkable.
The same reward circuits that are activated by addictive drugs light up when they look at a photo of their partner.
Meanwhile, levels of a chemical called serotonin can drop.
Low serotonin is linked to obsessive thinking.
That is why, when you fall for someone, you cannot stop thinking about them.
You replay every conversation.
You check your phone again and again.
And the part of the brain responsible for careful judgment and criticism becomes quieter.
In other words, your brain partly switches off the critic.
Love is not blind.
But in the beginning, it does wear very strong glasses.
Part Five.
From Spark to Bond.
Here is a problem.
That fire cannot burn forever.
A brain flooded with dopamine and obsession would be exhausted.
You still need to eat, sleep, and work.
So over months, the chemistry changes.
The wild excitement slowly calms down.
And if the relationship continues, two new chemicals take center stage.
The first is oxytocin, sometimes called the cuddle hormone.
It is released when people hug, hold hands, or spend close time together.
It builds trust and a feeling of safety.
The second is vasopressin, which is especially important in males.
In studies with small rodents called prairie voles, vasopressin helps males form long lasting bonds with a single partner.
When scientists blocked it, the bond did not form.
In humans, the picture is more complicated.
But the idea is similar.
Attraction is the spark.
Bonding is the fire that keeps you warm for years.
And there is a good evolutionary reason for this.
Human babies are incredibly helpless.
They need years of care.
For our ancestors, children with two caring parents had a better chance of survival.
So evolution did not just build men to be attracted to women.
It also built them to stay.
Part Six.
It Is Not Only Biology.
At this point, you might think attraction is just a program.
A set of instructions written in your genes and executed by chemicals.
But that is only half the story.
Because if attraction were purely biological, everyone would be attracted to exactly the same people.
And that is clearly not true.
Beauty standards change dramatically across cultures and across history.
In some times and places, a fuller body was a sign of wealth and good food.
In others, thinness became the ideal.
Fashion, media, and the people around you constantly shape what you find attractive.
Then there is familiarity.
Psychologists call it the mere exposure effect.
The more often you see someone, the more you tend to like them.
This is why so many people fall for a classmate, a neighbor, or a coworker.
Being close matters.
And then there is personality.
In large studies across dozens of countries, when people were asked what they want most in a long term partner,
the top answers were not looks or money.
They were kindness and intelligence.
A smile, a sense of humor, a warm voice, the way someone treats a stranger.
These things can make a person more attractive over time, even if they did not stand out at first glance.
So attraction is a conversation between two forces.
Ancient biology on one side.
Your personal life and culture on the other.
Part Seven.
You Are Not a Robot.
It is also important to remember that these are averages.
Patterns across thousands of people.
They are not rules for any single person.
Humans are wonderfully diverse.
Some men are attracted to men.
Some people feel little attraction at all.
Many people find themselves drawn to someone who does not match any checklist.
Evolution gave us tendencies, not orders.
And our big, complex brains allow us to choose, to reflect, and to love in ways that go far beyond our genes.
That is what makes human attraction so fascinating.
It is the meeting point of a billion years of evolution and a single moment in your own life.
Epilogue.
So let us go back to that street.
Hundreds of faces pass you by.
And then one of them stops you.
In that one second, your eyes read a face built by hormones and genes.
Your brain compares it to millions of faces you have seen before.
Your ears and your nose collect clues you will never notice.
Dopamine floods your reward system.
Your heart beats a little faster.
An ancient story, written over a billion years, plays out inside you in an instant.
But what happens next is not written in your genes.
Do you smile?
Do you say hello?
Do you walk away?
That part is up to you.
